newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower before election, refunding.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower before election, refunding.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Friday after profit-taking before the U.S. election and a big Treasury refunding next week wiped out an early advance scored on very moderate October U.S. payroll growth.

Prices climbed after the government reported that the economy created 210,000 new jobs in October. With a loss of 35,000 jobs in September, the pace of job growth in the first two months of the third quarter clearly showed moderation and diminished prospects for higher official interest rates.
The unemployment rate remained steady at 5.2 percent.
But the gains proved transitory.
Selling by central banks, hedge funds and general profit-taking erased the market's advance at mid-morning. Prices soon moved lower and they stayed in negative territory for the rest of the session.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 100-29/32, down 14/32, to yield 6.68 percent.
Still, the decline wiped out little more than half of Thursday's advance, when the bellwether 30-year bond rose 26/32, its yield falling to 6.64 percent, one of the lowest levels in seven months.

"This was nothing more than profit-taking," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and financial market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "It had nothing to do with how the market saw the October employment report. It was a little clearing of the decks before the (U.S.) election."
Sullivan said that in the campaign's waning days, "there's a little concern about the GOP (Republicans) losing control of one or more chambers of Congress, in particular the House.
"Rightly or wrongly, there's fear that the leadership of a Democratic House would be unwilling to address entitlements or to make more progress on narrowing the budget gap," he said.
Against that uncertainty, "traders were willing to ring up profits," Sullivan said.

Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said if the Republicans lose the House on Tuesday night, it will be "an overnight trade" worth a three-quarter point decline on the bond.
"It would take months and months to figure out whether Democrats were really going to be tax-and-spend liberals again," he said.
A positive aspect of the session was that the bond, despite its decline, held support above 100-23/32.
Rupkey said the reason that prices did not hold their gains on the friendly monthly payroll data is that the market has already priced in all the good news for miles around.

"We've discounted everything but the kitchen sink," he said. "We discounted a weaker economy and we got it. Realistically, people know inflation is dead and we've priced that in. There's no one left to buy."
The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said its October index eased a bit but remained above 50, a level that reflected moderate economic growth.
Sullivan said the Treasury's refunding next week should not present a great challenge to the market.
The Treasury will sell $18.5 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $10.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.

On Friday, bill rates finished higher with the three-month bill up one basis point to 5.03 percent, the six-month bill rate up two basis points to 5.09 percent and the year-bill rates up three basis points to 5.17 percent.
Two-year notes ended down 2/32 to 100-5/32, yielding 5.79 percent. Five-year notes finished off 5/32 to 100-19/32, yielding 6.11 percent.
Ten-year notes dropped 8/32 to close at 100-29/32, yielding 6.37 percent.
--North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
